claim: Rab26 is specifically associated with clusters of synaptic vesicles in neurites.
source: Here we show that Rab26 is specifically associated with clusters of synaptic vesicles in neurites.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data showing Rab26 localization in neurites (Figure 3), immunoisolation experiments (Figure 1), and electron microscopy observations (Figure 5).

claim: Overexpression of active but not GDP-preferring Rab26 enhances vesicle clustering.
source: Overexpression of active but not of GDP-preferring Rab26 enhances vesicle clustering, which is particularly conspicuous for the EGFP-tagged variant, resulting in a massive accumulation of synaptic vesicles in neuronal somata without altering the distribution of other organelles.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing FLAG-Rab26WT, FLAG-Rab26QL (active forms) with FLAG-Rab26TN (GDP-preferring) in neurons (Figure 3C-E) and by EGFP-Rab26WT overexpression (Figure 4).

claim: EGFP-tagged Rab26 results in massive accumulation of synaptic vesicles in neuronal somata without altering the distribution of other organelles.
source: Overexpression of active but not of GDP-preferring Rab26 enhances vesicle clustering, which is particularly conspicuous for the EGFP-tagged variant, resulting in a massive accumulation of synaptic vesicles in neuronal somata without altering the distribution of other organelles.
evidence: Immunofluorescence shows EGFP-Rab26WT forms large clusters in soma that colocalize with synaptic vesicle markers but not with early endosomes or Golgi (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: Both endogenous and induced Rab26 clusters co-localize with autophagy-related proteins such as Atg16L1, LC3B and Rab33B.
source: Both endogenous and induced clusters co-localize with autophagy-related proteins such as Atg16L1, LC3B and Rab33B but not with other organelles.
evidence: Immunofluorescence microscopy demonstrates colocalization of Rab26 with Atg16L1 (Figure 6A-C), LC3B (Figure 6D), and Rab33B (Figure 6E-F).

claim: Rab26 clusters do not co-localize with other organelles.
source: Both endogenous and induced clusters co-localize with autophagy-related proteins such as Atg16L1, LC3B and Rab33B but not with other organelles.
evidence: Immunofluorescence shows no overlap with early endosomes (EEA1) or Golgi (GM130) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).

claim: Atg16L1 is a direct effector of Rab26.
source: Furthermore, Atg16L1 appears to be a direct effector of Rab26 and binds Rab26 in its GTP-bound form, albeit only with low affinity.
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation (Figure 7A) and GST pulldown assays (Figure 7B) demonstrate GTP-dependent binding between Rab26 and Atg16L1.

claim: Atg16L1 binds Rab26 in its GTP-bound form with low affinity.
source: Furthermore, Atg16L1 appears to be a direct effector of Rab26 and binds Rab26 in its GTP-bound form, albeit only with low affinity.
evidence: Analytical gel filtration failed to detect stable Rab26-Atg16L1 complexes while Rab33-Atg16L1 complexes were detectable (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), suggesting weaker binding.

claim: Rab26 selectively directs synaptic and secretory vesicles into preautophagosomal structures.
source: We propose that Rab26 selectively directs synaptic and secretory vesicles into preautophagosomal structures, suggesting the presence of a novel pathway for degradation of synaptic vesicles.
evidence: This is inferred from colocalization with autophagy markers (Figure 6), electron microscopy showing vesicle clusters surrounded by isolation membranes (Figure 5), and the presence of both synaptic and dense-core vesicle markers in clusters (Figure 4).

claim: There is a novel pathway for degradation of synaptic vesicles involving Rab26.
source: We propose that Rab26 selectively directs synaptic and secretory vesicles into preautophagosomal structures, suggesting the presence of a novel pathway for degradation of synaptic vesicles.
evidence: The proposal is based on the association of Rab26 with autophagy machinery and vesicle clusters, suggesting a selective autophagy pathway termed 'vesiculophagy'.

claim: Rab26 co-purifies with synaptic vesicles during biochemical fractionation from rat brain.
source: As shown in Figure 1A, Rab26 co-purified with synaptic vesicle markers (as indicated here using synaptophysin), with the highest enrichment being observed in the synaptic vesicle (SV) fraction obtained after purification using consecutive density gradients and size exclusion chromatography.
evidence: Immunoblotting of subcellular fractions shows Rab26 enrichment parallels synaptophysin enrichment in the SV fraction (Figure 1A).

claim: The synaptic vesicle fraction obtained after purification using consecutive density gradients and size exclusion chromatography has been previously shown to be comprised almost exclusively of synaptic vesicles (at least 95% purity).
source: This fraction has been previously shown to be comprised almost exclusively of synaptic vesicles (at least 95% purity) (Huttner et al., 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by Huttner et al., 1983.

claim: Immunoisolation using Rab26 or synaptophysin antibodies results in isolation of membranes highly enriched in both synaptophysin and Rab26.
source: As shown in Figure 1B, both antibodies resulted in the isolation of membranes highly enriched in both synaptophysin and Rab26.
evidence: Immunoblotting of immunoisolated material shows both Rab26 and synaptophysin are present regardless of which antibody was used for isolation (Figure 1B).

claim: Synaptophysin-beads are densely covered by small vesicular profiles with a size distribution typical for synaptic vesicles (40–45 nm).
source: As previously reported, synaptophysin-beads were densely covered by small vesicular profiles with a size distribution typical for synaptic vesicles (i.e., 40–45 nm) (Figure 1C) (Burger et al., 1989; Takamori et al., 2000).
evidence: Electron microscopy images show vesicles bound to synaptophysin beads (Figure 1C) and size distribution analysis confirms 40-45 nm peak (Figure 1E).

claim: Rab26 beads are populated with vesicles similar to those on synaptophysin beads, albeit to a lesser extent.
source: Rab26 beads were similarly populated with these vesicles, albeit to a lesser extent (Figure 1D).
evidence: Electron microscopy shows vesicles on Rab26 beads (Figure 1D) with similar size distribution to synaptophysin beads (Figure 1E).

claim: The size distribution of vesicles bound to synaptophysin and Rab26 beads is indistinguishable.
source: Nevertheless, quantitative assessment of the size distribution of the bead-bound vesicles revealed no distinguishable difference between the vesicles bound to synaptophysin and Rab26 beads, respectively (Figure 1E).
evidence: Quantitative size distribution analysis shows overlapping profiles for both bead types (Figure 1E).

claim: Rab26 is resistant to extraction by GDI from synaptic vesicle membranes.
source: By comparison, Rab26 is resistant to GDI-mediated membrane extraction, even when GDP is present in excess (Figure 2A).
evidence: Biochemical assay shows Rab26 remains membrane-associated after GDI treatment while Rab3 is extracted (Figure 2A).

claim: Rab3 is rapidly retrieved from synaptic vesicles membranes by GDI in the presence of GDP.
source: Consistent with previous observations, Rab3 is rapidly retrieved from synaptic vesicles membranes by GDI in the presence of GDP (Araki et al., 1990; Chou and Jahn, 2000; Pavlos et al., 2010).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the GDI extraction assay (Figure 2A) and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Rab26's resistance to GDI-mediated membrane extraction is reminiscent of Rab27b.
source: This feature is reminiscent of the biochemical characteristics of Rab27b, which also fails to be retrieved from synaptic vesicles by GDI treatment in vitro (Pavlos et al., 2010).
evidence: This comparison is supported by citation to previous work on Rab27b (Pavlos et al., 2010).

claim: Rab27b dimerizes and persists on synaptic vesicle membranes in its GDP-bound form.
source: Rather, Rab27b is known to dimerize and persist on synaptic vesicle membranes in its GDP-bound form (Chavas et al., 2007; Pavlos et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Rab26 oligomerizes preferentially in its GDP-bound form.
source: Together, these data indicate that Rab26 is a synaptic vesicle protein that oligomerizes preferentially in its GDP-bound form, thereby precluding GDI-mediated membrane extraction—a feature shared with its synaptic vesicle relative Rab27b.
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments show FLAG-Rab26 co-precipitates with EGFP-Rab26WT and more efficiently with Rab26TN (GDP-preferring), but not with Rab26QL (GTP-locked) (Figure 2B).

claim: Co-precipitation of FLAG-tagged Rab26 is observed when cells are transfected with either wild-type EGFP-Rab26 or with a GDP-preferring variant (Rab26T77N).
source: As shown in Figure 2B, co-precipitation of FLAG-tagged Rab26 was only observed when cells were transfected with either wild-type EGFP-Rab26 or with a GDP-preferring variant (Rab26T77N, henceforth referred to as Rab26TN).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data shows binding between FLAG-Rab26WT and EGFP-Rab26WT or EGFP-Rab26TN (Figure 2B).

claim: Little to no co-precipitation of FLAG-Rab26 is observable when the 'nucleotide empty' Rab26 (Rab26N177I) or 'GTP-locked' (Rab26Q123L) variants are employed.
source: By comparison, little to no co-precipitation was observable when the 'nucleotide empty' Rab26 (Rab26N177I, Rab26NI) or 'GTP-locked' (Rab26Q123L, Rab26QL) variants were employed.
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation shows reduced or absent binding with Rab26NI and Rab26QL (Figure 2B).

claim: Endogenous Rab26 exhibits a conspicuous punctate staining pattern that overlaps with, although is not identical to, synaptotagmin-I.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, Rab26 labeling resulted in a conspicuous punctate staining pattern that overlapped with, although was not identical to, the pattern obtained with synaptotagmin-I antibodies.
evidence: Immunofluorescence microscopy shows partial colocalization between Rab26 and synaptotagmin-I in neurons (Figure 3A,B).

claim: Most Rab26 positive puncta colocalize with synaptotagmin-I in neurites.
source: Higher magnification of neurites revealed that most of the Rab26 positive puncta colocalized with synaptotagmin-I.
evidence: High magnification imaging shows colocalization of Rab26 and synaptotagmin-I puncta (Figure 3B, arrows).

claim: Many puncta positive for synaptotagmin-I are not stained with the Rab26 antibody.
source: In contrast, many puncta positive for synaptotagmin-I were not stained with the Rab26 antibody (Figure 3B, arrows show colocalization).
evidence: Immunofluorescence shows synaptotagmin-I puncta without Rab26 staining (Figure 3B).

claim: FLAG-Rab26WT and FLAG-Rab26QL co-localize with a subset of synaptotagmin positive puncta in neurites.
source: The staining pattern obtained with Rab26WT (Figure 3C) and with Rab26QL (the GTP-preferring variant) (Figure 3D) was very similar to that of endogenous Rab26, showing a high degree of overlap with endogenous synaptotagmin 1.
evidence: Immunofluorescence of transfected neurons shows colocalization of FLAG-Rab26WT and FLAG-Rab26QL with synaptotagmin-I (Figure 3C,D).

claim: FLAG-Rab26TN exhibits a more diffuse but still somewhat granular pattern that displays no significant co-localization with synaptotagmin 1.
source: In contrast, the GDP-preferring Rab26TN exhibited a more diffuse but still somewhat granular pattern that displayed no significant co-localization with synaptotagmin 1 (Figure 3E).
evidence: Immunofluorescence shows FLAG-Rab26TN has diffuse distribution without colocalization with synaptotagmin-I (Figure 3E).

claim: EGFP-tagged wildtype Rab26 colocalizes with synaptic vesicle markers including synaptophysin.
source: A similar staining pattern was also observed when EGFP-tagged wildtype Rab26 was used, with the fusion protein again colocalizing with synaptic vesicle markers (in this case synaptophysin) (Figure 3F)
evidence: Immunofluorescence shows EGFP-Rab26WT colocalizes with synaptophysin in neurites (Figure 3F).

claim: EGFP-Rab26WT colocalizes with the neuropeptide RFP-NPY.
source: A similar staining pattern was also observed when EGFP-tagged wildtype Rab26 was used, with the fusion protein again colocalizing with synaptic vesicle markers (in this case synaptophysin) (Figure 3F) and with the neuropeptide RFP-NPY but not with the early endosomal marker/Rab5 effector EEA1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B, respectively).
evidence: Immunofluorescence shows colocalization between EGFP-Rab26WT and RFP-NPY (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).

claim: EGFP-Rab26WT does not colocalize with the early endosomal marker/Rab5 effector EEA1.
source: A similar staining pattern was also observed when EGFP-tagged wildtype Rab26 was used, with the fusion protein again colocalizing with synaptic vesicle markers (in this case synaptophysin) (Figure 3F) and with the neuropeptide RFP-NPY but not with the early endosomal marker/Rab5 effector EEA1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B, respectively).
evidence: Immunofluorescence shows no overlap between EGFP-Rab26WT and EEA1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Rab26 likely traffics in a pathway distinct from Rab5.
source: This suggests that Rab26 is likely to traffic in a pathway distinct from Rab5.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of colocalization with EEA1, a Rab5 effector (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Many EGFP-Rab26 puncta colocalize with vesicles labeled with antibody against the luminal domain of synaptotagmin-I.
source: As shown in Figure 3G, many of the EGFP-Rab26 puncta colocalized with vesicles labeled with this antibody, thereby confirming that these Rab26-positive vesicles originated from endocytosis of vesicles that previously had undergone at least one round of exocytosis.
evidence: Live cell imaging with luminal synaptotagmin-I antibody shows colocalization with EGFP-Rab26WT puncta (Figure 3G).

claim: Rab26-positive vesicles originated from endocytosis of vesicles that previously had undergone at least one round of exocytosis.
source: As shown in Figure 3G, many of the EGFP-Rab26 puncta colocalized with vesicles labeled with this antibody, thereby confirming that these Rab26-positive vesicles originated from endocytosis of vesicles that previously had undergone at least one round of exocytosis.
evidence: Colocalization with luminal synaptotagmin-I antibody (which only labels vesicles that have undergone exocytosis) confirms recycling (Figure 3G).

claim: Rab26 is one of the Rab GTPases conserved between mammals and Drosophila.
source: Rab26 is one of the Rab GTPases conserved between mammals and Drosophila, with the genome of latter encoding three alternatively spliced isoforms.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Rab26 conservation.

claim: The Drosophila genome encodes three alternatively spliced isoforms of Rab26.
source: Rab26 is one of the Rab GTPases conserved between mammals and Drosophila, with the genome of latter encoding three alternatively spliced isoforms.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Drosophila Rab26.

claim: Rab26 is expressed specifically in neurons at all developmental stages in Drosophila (larval and pupal development, adult flies).
source: According to a systematic analysis of all Drosophila Rab proteins, Rab26 is expressed specifically in neurons at all developmental stages (larval and pupal development, adults flies) (Chan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chan et al., 2011.

claim: Expression of YFP-tagged Rab26 variants in Drosophila using the pan neuronal elav-Gal4 driver causes no lethality or delayed development.
source: Although the tagged Rab26 protein variants were expressed throughout development, no lethality or delayed development was observed (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments.

claim: Rab26 localizes exclusively to presynaptic compartments of the neuromuscular junction in Drosophila without staining of axons and cell bodies.
source: Consistent with previous observations, analysis of third instar larvae nerve-muscle preparations revealed an exclusive localization of Rab26 to presynaptic compartments of the neuromuscular junction without staining of axons and cell bodies (Figure 3—figure supplement 2; see also [Chan et al., 2011]).
evidence: Immunofluorescence of Drosophila NMJs shows Rab26 localization to presynaptic compartments (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), consistent with previous work (Chan et al., 2011).

claim: Expression of wild-type and gain-of-function (QL) Rab26 in Drosophila results in the appearance of large vesicle clusters within presynaptic boutons.
source: Remarkably, expression of wild-type and of the gain-of-function (QL) Rab26 resulted in the appearance of large vesicle clusters within the presynaptic boutons whereas the GDP-preferring form (TN) was diffusely localized.
evidence: Immunofluorescence of Drosophila NMJs shows large Rab26-positive clusters with WT and QL variants but not TN (Figure 3H).

claim: The GDP-preferring form of Rab26 (TN) is diffusely localized in Drosophila presynaptic boutons.
source: Remarkably, expression of wild-type and of the gain-of-function (QL) Rab26 resulted in the appearance of large vesicle clusters within the presynaptic boutons whereas the GDP-preferring form (TN) was diffusely localized.
evidence: Immunofluorescence shows diffuse distribution of Rab26TN in Drosophila NMJs (Figure 3H).

claim: Formation of Rab26 clusters in Drosophila is dependent on the nucleotide-bound state of Rab26.
source: This indicated that, like in hippocampal neurons, formation of these clusters is dependent on the nucleotide-bound state of Rab26 (Figure 3H).
evidence: Comparison of WT/QL (clustered) versus TN (diffuse) variants indicates nucleotide-dependence (Figure 3H).

claim: Rab26-positive compartments in Drosophila NMJs are present in boutons as indicated by staining with anti-horseradish peroxidase (HRP).
source: These Rab26-positive compartments are present in neuromuscular junction boutons as indicated by staining with anti-horseradish peroxidase (HRP) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Immunofluorescence shows colocalization of Rab26 with HRP, a presynaptic membrane marker (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: Rab26-positive compartments in Drosophila show partial overlap with the synaptic vesicle protein cysteine string protein (Csp).
source: and showed a partial overlap with the synaptic vesicle protein cysteine string protein (Csp) (Figure 3H) (Zinsmaier et al., 1990).
evidence: Immunofluorescence shows partial colocalization between Rab26 and Csp (Figure 3H).

claim: Large Rab26-positive structures in Drosophila often show intense Csp staining at their borders.
source: Conspicuously, large Rab26-positive structures often showed intense Csp staining at their borders.
evidence: Immunofluorescence observations show Csp enrichment at borders of Rab26 clusters (Figure 3H).

claim: Rab26 is excluded from active zones immunostained for Bruchpilot (Brp) in Drosophila.
source: Importantly, Rab26 is excluded from active zones immunostained for the Bruchpilot (Brp), a scaffold protein specifically localized to active zones (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) (Wagh et al., 2006).
evidence: Immunofluorescence shows no overlap between Rab26 and Bruchpilot (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: Expression of EGFP-Rab26WT in cultured hippocampal neurons results in a unique and highly conspicuous phenotype not observed with endogenous Rab26, untagged or FLAG-tagged Rab26.
source: Whereas the distribution of endogenous and tagged-expressing Rab26 variants was comparable in neurites, expression of EGFP-Rab26WT in cultured hippocampal neurons resulted in a unique and highly conspicuous phenotype that was not observed with endogenous Rab26, untagged or FLAG-tagged Rab26 and that has not been previously reported for any other EGFP-tagged Rab GTPase.
evidence: Comparison of immunofluorescence patterns shows EGFP-Rab26WT induces large somatic clusters not seen with other Rab26 forms (Figures 3, 4).

claim: The EGFP-Rab26WT phenotype has not been previously reported for any other EGFP-tagged Rab GTPase.
source: Whereas the distribution of endogenous and tagged-expressing Rab26 variants was comparable in neurites, expression of EGFP-Rab26WT in cultured hippocampal neurons resulted in a unique and highly conspicuous phenotype that was not observed with endogenous Rab26, untagged or FLAG-tagged Rab26 and that has not been previously reported for any other EGFP-tagged Rab GTPase.
evidence: This is stated as a novel observation in the context of Rab GTPase research.

claim: EGFP-Rab26WT induces the formation of large vesicular structures in the soma that can fill the major part of the neuronal cytoplasm.
source: In the soma, EGFP-Rab26WT induced the formation of large vesicular structures that, in some instances, filled the major part of the neuronal cytoplasm (Figure 4).
evidence: Immunofluorescence microscopy shows large EGFP-Rab26WT-positive structures in neuronal soma (Figure 4).

claim: EGFP-Rab26WT-induced structures are intensely positive for both synaptic vesicle and large dense core vesicle markers.
source: These structures were intensely positive for both synaptic vesicle (Figure 4A,B) and large dense core vesicle markers, that is, the two types of neuronal secretory vesicles that usually do not show significant overlap (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Immunofluorescence shows colocalization of EGFP-Rab26WT clusters with synaptobrevin, Rab3a (Figure 4A,B), RFP-NPY (Figure 4C), and Secretogranin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Synaptic vesicles and large dense core vesicles usually do not show significant overlap.
source: These structures were intensely positive for both synaptic vesicle (Figure 4A,B) and large dense core vesicle markers, that is, the two types of neuronal secretory vesicles that usually do not show significant overlap (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about vesicle marker distribution.

claim: The overlap between EGFP-Rab26WT clusters and Rab3A is less apparent than with other synaptic vesicle markers.
source: Intriguingly, the overlap with Rab3A, the major Rab-GTPase associated with synaptic vesicles, was less apparent.
evidence: Immunofluorescence shows reduced colocalization between EGFP-Rab26WT and Rab3a compared to other markers (Figure 4B).

claim: EGFP-Rab26WT clusters show no overlap with early endosomes or Golgi.
source: Double labeling with a variety of compartment-specific markers revealed no overlap with early endosomes or Golgi (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B, respectively)
evidence: Immunofluorescence shows no colocalization with EEA1 or GM130 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).

claim: EGFP-Rab26WT clusters show some, albeit limited, overlap with lysosomes.
source: Double labeling with a variety of compartment-specific markers revealed no overlap with early endosomes or Golgi (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B, respectively) but some, albeit limited, overlap with lysosomes (Figure 4D).
evidence: Immunofluorescence shows partial colocalization with LAMP2, a lysosomal marker (Figure 4D).

claim: The soma of neurons expressing EGFP-Rab26WT contains large clusters of numerous small vesicles that are positive for both EGFP-Rab26WT and synaptobrevin.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, the soma contained large clusters of numerous small vesicles that were positive for both EGFP-Rab26WT and synaptobrevin (Sybv).
evidence: Immunogold-TEM shows clusters of small vesicles labeled with both EGFP and synaptobrevin antibodies (Figure 5A).

claim: EGFP-Rab26WT-induced vesicle clusters are rather homogenous but occasionally contain larger vesicles and mitochondria.
source: In many cases, these clusters were rather homogenous, but occasionally also contained larger vesicles and mitochondria (Figure 5B).
evidence: Electron microscopy shows clusters with predominantly small vesicles but occasional larger vesicles and mitochondria (Figure 5B).

claim: Some EGFP-Rab26WT-induced vesicle clusters reach enormous dimensions containing possibly 1000s of small vesicles.
source: Although no systematic quantification was performed, some of these clusters reached enormous dimensions containing possibly 1000s of small vesicles (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Electron microscopy shows very large clusters of vesicles (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: Some EGFP-Rab26WT-induced vesicle clusters are surrounded by a single and/or double membrane.
source: In some cases, these clusters were surrounded by a single and/or double membrane (Figure 5C, inset), although this was somewhat variable.
evidence: Electron microscopy shows membrane(s) surrounding some clusters (Figure 5C, inset).

claim: Neuromuscular junctions of Drosophila strains overexpressing YFP-Rab26WT show dense clusters of vesicles devoid of surrounding membranes that are clearly set apart from surrounding synaptic vesicles.
source: Here, dense clusters of vesicles (devoid of surrounding membranes) were regularly observable that were clearly set apart from surrounding synaptic vesicles (Figure 5D, indicated by an arrow) but were clearly absent in controls.
evidence: Electron microscopy of Drosophila NMJs shows vesicle clusters in YFP-Rab26WT expressing animals but not controls (Figure 5D).

claim: An almost perfect colocalization between Atg16L1 and EGFP-Rab26WT-positive clusters is detected in neuronal cell bodies.
source: Indeed, an almost perfect colocalization between Atg16L1 and Rab26-positive clusters was detected in neuronal cell bodies (Figure 6A), thereby identifying these clusters as autophagosomal precursors.
evidence: Immunofluorescence shows extensive colocalization between EGFP-Rab26WT and endogenous Atg16L1 in soma (Figure 6A).

claim: Colocalization between Atg16L1 and Rab26-positive clusters identifies these clusters as autophagosomal precursors.
source: Indeed, an almost perfect colocalization between Atg16L1 and Rab26-positive clusters was detected in neuronal cell bodies (Figure 6A), thereby identifying these clusters as autophagosomal precursors.
evidence: The colocalization with Atg16L1, a pre-autophagosome marker, is used to infer the identity of the clusters.

claim: A high degree of overlap is observed between endogenous Rab26 and Atg16L1 in clusters decorating neurites.
source: Next, we stained untransfected neurons for endogenous Rab26 and Atg16L1. Again, a high degree of overlap was observed between Rab26 and Atg16L1 in clusters decorating neurites (Figure 6B) but not in cell bodies which remained largely unstained (not shown).
evidence: Immunofluorescence of untransfected neurons shows colocalization of endogenous Rab26 and Atg16L1 in neurites (Figure 6B).

claim: Strong overlap with Atg16L1 is observed when neurons are transfected with FLAG-Rab26WT and/or FLAG-Rab26QL, but not with FLAG-Rab26TN.
source: Strong overlap with Atg16L1 was also observed when neurons were transfected with FLAG-Rab26WT and/or FLAG-Rab26QL, but not with FLAG-Rab26TN (Figure 6C).
evidence: Immunofluorescence shows colocalization of Atg16L1 with FLAG-Rab26WT and FLAG-Rab26QL but not FLAG-Rab26TN (Figure 6C).

claim: The association of Rab26 with autophagosomes depends on the GTP-form of the protein.
source: This indicated that the association of Rab26 with autophagosomes depends on the GTP-form of the protein.
evidence: Differential colocalization with Atg16L1 between GTP-bound (WT/QL) and GDP-bound (TN) forms indicates GTP-dependence (Figure 6C).

claim: Overexpression of GTP-bound forms (WT and QL), but not GDP-bound (TN) form, of EGFP-Rab26 in HeLa cells leads to the formation of large Atg16L1-positive clusters.
source: This GTP-dependency was similarly noted in HeLa cells following ectopic expression of Rab26. In this instance, overexpression of GTP-bound forms (WT and QL), but not GDP-bound (TN) form, of EGFP-Rab26 led to the formation of large Atg16L1-positive clusters (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Immunofluorescence of HeLa cells shows Atg16L1-positive clusters with EGFP-Rab26WT and EGFP-Rab26QL but not EGFP-Rab26TN (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-C).

claim: Clusters in HeLa cells expressing EGFP-Rab26WT consist of small but often heterogeneous vesicles, partially surrounded by membranes, with EGFP labeling detected both on vesicles within clusters and on their encapsulating membrane(s).
source: Analysis by immunogold-TEM again revealed that these clusters consisted of small but often heterogeneous vesicles, partially surrounded by membranes, with EGFP labeling detected both on vesicles within clusters as well as on their encapsulating membrane(s) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Immunogold-TEM of HeLa cells shows vesicle clusters with EGFP labeling on vesicles and surrounding membranes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Co-expression of GFP-LC3 and active forms FLAG-Rab26 (WT and QL) results in a localization pattern comparable to that observed for Atg16L1.
source: Co-expression of GFP-LC3 and active forms FLAG-Rab26 (WT and QL) resulted in a localization pattern comparable to that observed for Atg16L1 (Figure 6D), thereby verifying the nature of these compartments as autophagosomes.
evidence: Immunofluorescence shows colocalization of GFP-LC3B with FLAG-Rab26WT and FLAG-Rab26QL in neurites (Figure 6D).

claim: Colocalization of LC3 with Rab26 clusters verifies the nature of these compartments as autophagosomes.
source: Co-expression of GFP-LC3 and active forms FLAG-Rab26 (WT and QL) resulted in a localization pattern comparable to that observed for Atg16L1 (Figure 6D), thereby verifying the nature of these compartments as autophagosomes.
evidence: LC3 is a canonical autophagosome marker, so its colocalization with Rab26 clusters confirms their autophagosomal identity.

claim: LC3 recruitment is not observed when EGFP-tagged Rab26WT is overexpressed.
source: Interestingly, however, LC3 recruitment was not observed when the EGFP-tagged Rab26WT was overexpressed (not shown, see 'Discussion').
evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments not shown.

claim: There is a growing body of evidence implicating several Rabs (Rab1, Rab7, Rab9, Rab11, Rab24, Rab32, and Rab33) in canonical autophagy.
source: Indeed, there is now a growing body evidence implicating several Rabs (Rab1, Rab7, Rab9, Rab11, Rab24, Rab32, and Rab33, inclusive) in canonical autophagy (for a comprehensive review [Chua et al., 2011]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a comprehensive review (Chua et al., 2011).

claim: Rab33, a Golgi resident Rab, participates in the formation of autophagosome precursors by recruiting Atg16L1 to isolation membranes.
source: Among these, Rab33, a Golgi resident Rab, participates in the formation of autophagosome precursors by recruiting Atg16L1 (a Rab33 effector) to isolation membranes (Itoh et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Itoh et al., 2008.

claim: Atg16L1 is a Rab33 effector.
source: Among these, Rab33, a Golgi resident Rab, participates in the formation of autophagosome precursors by recruiting Atg16L1 (a Rab33 effector) to isolation membranes (Itoh et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Itoh et al., 2008.

claim: EGFP-Rab33BWT is largely restricted to the perinuclear/Golgi region in the soma with no appreciable overlap with FLAG-Rab26WT.
source: As shown in Figure 6E, EGFP-Rab33BWT was largely restricted to the perinuclear/Golgi region in the soma which showed no appreciable overlap with FLAG-Rab26WT.
evidence: Immunofluorescence shows EGFP-Rab33BWT in perinuclear region without overlap with FLAG-Rab26WT in soma (Figure 6E).

claim: Significant overlap between Rab26 and Rab33 is observed in peripheral puncta lining neurites.
source: On the other hand, significant overlap between Rab26 and Rab33 was observed in more peripheral puncta lining neurites (Figure 6F).
evidence: Immunofluorescence shows colocalization of FLAG-Rab26WT and EGFP-Rab33BWT in neurites (Figure 6F).

claim: The autophagy-pathway regulated by Rab26 may functionally intersect with Rab33.
source: Together these data imply that the autophagy-pathway regulated by Rab26 may functionally intersect with Rab33.
evidence: This is inferred from the colocalization of Rab26 and Rab33 in neurites and their shared interaction with Atg16L1.

claim: Endogenous Atg16L1 co-precipitates with FLAG-Rab26QL but not with FLAG-Rab26WT or FLAG-Rab26TN.
source: Immunoblotting for endogenous Atg16L1 from the same immunoprecipitates revealed co-precipitation between Atg16L1 and Rab26QL. By comparison, little to no Atg16L1 was detectable in the precipitates of Rab26-WT and Rab26TN, respectively, indicating that the interaction between Rab26 and Atg16L1 is GTP-dependent.
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation shows Atg16L1 binding to FLAG-Rab26QL but not to FLAG-Rab26WT or FLAG-Rab26TN (Figure 7A).

claim: The interaction between Rab26 and Atg16L1 is GTP-dependent.
source: Immunoblotting for endogenous Atg16L1 from the same immunoprecipitates revealed co-precipitation between Atg16L1 and Rab26QL. By comparison, little to no Atg16L1 was detectable in the precipitates of Rab26-WT and Rab26TN, respectively, indicating that the interaction between Rab26 and Atg16L1 is GTP-dependent.
evidence: Selective binding to Rab26QL (GTP-preferring) but not Rab26TN (GDP-preferring) indicates GTP-dependence (Figure 7A).

claim: GST-pulldown reveals an interaction between Atg16L1 and Rab26, with Atg16L1 binding to the QL and to a lesser extent the TN-variant of Rab26.
source: In agreement with our immunoprecipitation studies, GST-pulldown revealed an interaction between Atg16L1 and Rab26, with Atg16L1 binding to the QL and to a lesser extent the TN-variant of Rab26 (Figure 7B), with the latter being further reduced upon repetitive washings (not shown).
evidence: GST pulldown assay shows binding of Atg16NT/Atg5 complex to GST-Rab26QL and weaker binding to GST-Rab26TN (Figure 7B).

claim: Binding of Atg16L1 to Rab26TN is further reduced upon repetitive washings.
source: In agreement with our immunoprecipitation studies, GST-pulldown revealed an interaction between Atg16L1 and Rab26, with Atg16L1 binding to the QL and to a lesser extent the TN-variant of Rab26 (Figure 7B), with the latter being further reduced upon repetitive washings (not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments not shown.

claim: Formation of Rab26(QL)-ATG16L1 complexes is not detectable by analytical gel filtration.
source: Surprisingly, formation of Rab26(QL)-ATG16L1 complexes were not detectable with this approach (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Gel filtration analysis shows no co-migration of Rab26QL with Atg16NT/Atg5 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Complex formation between Rab33(QL) and ATG16L1 is detectable by analytical gel filtration.
source: As a positive control, we carried out the same experiment using Rab33(QL) and ATG16L1. Here, complex formation was detectable with this approach.
evidence: Gel filtration analysis shows co-migration of Rab33QL with Atg16NT/Atg5 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).

claim: RAB26 binds ATG16L1 in a GTP-dependent manner, but this binding appears to be weaker than the interaction between Rab33 and ATG16L1.
source: Thus, while both IP and pull-down experiments show that RAB26 binds ATG16L1 in a GTP-dependent manner, this binding appears to be weaker than the interaction between Rab33 and ATG16L1.
evidence: This is inferred from the positive IP and pulldown results but negative gel filtration results for Rab26-Atg16L1, contrasted with positive gel filtration for Rab33-Atg16L1.

claim: Rab26 is most closely related to the secretory GTPases Rab3 and Rab27.
source: Rab26 is most closely related to the secretory GTPases Rab3 and Rab27, which led to the conclusion that it may perform similar functions in membrane traffic (Fukuda, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fukuda, 2008.

claim: Rab26 is associated with zymogen granules in exocrine cells.
source: This view is supported by reports showing association of Rab26 with zymogen granules in exocrine cells (Nashida et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nashida et al., 2006.

claim: Overexpression of the dominant-negative form of Rab26 abolishes the formation of zymogen granules.
source: and by the observation that overexpression of the dominant-negative form abolishes the formation of zymogen granules (Tian et al., 2010; Li et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tian et al., 2010 and Li et al., 2012.

claim: Rab26 has been found to be associated with lysosomes in zymogen-secreting cells.
source: More recently, Rab26 has been found to be associated with lysosomes in zymogen-secreting cells (Jin and Mills, 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jin and Mills, 2014.

claim: The functions of Rab26 in secretory cells extend beyond that of exocytosis.
source: More recently, Rab26 has been found to be associated with lysosomes in zymogen-secreting cells (Jin and Mills, 2014) implying that its functions in secretory cells extend beyond that of exocytosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the association with lysosomes, which are degradative organelles.

claim: Rab26 was identified among the list of Rab proteins (up-to-30) enriched on highly purified synaptic vesicles in previous proteomic studies.
source: In our previous work (Takamori et al., 2006; Pavlos et al., 2010), Rab26 was identified among the list of Rab proteins (up-to-30) enriched on highly purified synaptic vesicles.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors (Takamori et al., 2006; Pavlos et al., 2010).

claim: The association of Rab26 with synaptic vesicles is exclusive, with Rab26 being absent from other organelles such as early endosomes.
source: Our present data now show that this association is exclusive, with Rab26 being absent from other organelles such as early endosomes, paralleling the distribution of other secretory Rabs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by lack of colocalization with EEA1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).

claim: The preferential association of Rab26 with large clusters of synaptic vesicles and its conspicuous absence from smaller boutons positive for synaptic vesicle markers is clearly distinct from Rab3 and Rab27b.
source: On the other hand, the preferential association of Rab26 with large clusters of synaptic vesicles and its conspicuous absence from smaller boutons positive for synaptic vesicle markers is clearly distinct from Rab3 and Rab27b and indicates that Rab26 may not be contributing to the canonical function of these Rabs in regulated exocytosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the distinct localization pattern of Rab26 compared to Rab3 (Figure 4B shows less overlap with Rab3a).

claim: Rab26 may not be contributing to the canonical function of Rab3 and Rab27b in regulated exocytosis.
source: On the other hand, the preferential association of Rab26 with large clusters of synaptic vesicles and its conspicuous absence from smaller boutons positive for synaptic vesicle markers is clearly distinct from Rab3 and Rab27b and indicates that Rab26 may not be contributing to the canonical function of these Rabs in regulated exocytosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the distinct localization pattern and association with autophagy markers rather than active zones.

claim: Rab11 and Rab9 crystallize as dimers in the GDP-state.
source: Rather, Rab26 exhibits a tendency to oligomerize in the GDP-form, again a feature shared with Rab27b and perhaps with some others such as Rab11 and Rab9, which crystallize as dimers in the GDP-state (Pasqualato et al., 2004; Wittmann and Rudolph, 2004; Chavas et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies (Pasqualato et al., 2004; Wittmann and Rudolph, 2004; Chavas et al., 2007).

claim: Wild-type Rab proteins have high intrinsic GTP-hydrolysis rates.
source: However, this might be explained by the known high intrinsic GTP-hydrolysis rates of wild-type and native Rab proteins which would render a percentage of wild-type Rab26 inactive (approximately 40% by co-immunoprecipitation), thereby prompting its oligomerization on membranes and hence preclude its GDI-extraction from synaptic vesicles.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Rab protein biochemistry.

claim: Approximately 40% of wild-type Rab26 is inactive (GDP-bound) as determined by co-immunoprecipitation.
source: However, this might be explained by the known high intrinsic GTP-hydrolysis rates of wild-type and native Rab proteins which would render a percentage of wild-type Rab26 inactive (approximately 40% by co-immunoprecipitation), thereby prompting its oligomerization on membranes and hence preclude its GDI-extraction from synaptic vesicles.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-immunoprecipitation data showing partial oligomerization of wild-type Rab26 (Figure 2B).

claim: The propensity of Rab26TN to rapidly oligomerize would likely result in a steric clash with the GDI-related Rab escort protein (REP), which is required for prenylation and delivery of newly synthesized Rabs to their cognate membranes.
source: By comparison, the propensity of the 'GDP-locked' variant (Rab26TN) to rapidly oligomerize would likely result a steric clash with the GDI-related Rab escort protein (REP), which is required for prenylation and delivery of new synthesized Rabs to their cognate membranes (Andres et al., 1993).
evidence: This is speculated based on known REP function (Andres et al., 1993) and the oligomerization tendency of Rab26TN.

claim: REP is required for prenylation and delivery of newly synthesized Rabs to their cognate membranes.
source: By comparison, the propensity of the 'GDP-locked' variant (Rab26TN) to rapidly oligomerize would likely result a steric clash with the GDI-related Rab escort protein (REP), which is required for prenylation and delivery of new synthesized Rabs to their cognate membranes (Andres et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Andres et al., 1993.

claim: The predominantly cytosolic distribution pattern of FLAG/EGFP-tagged Rab26TN is consistent with a steric clash with REP preventing membrane delivery.
source: Such a scenario would be in keeping with the predominantly cytosolic distribution pattern observed in neurons expressing FLAG/EGFP-tagged Rab26TN.
evidence: This is inferred from the diffuse distribution of Rab26TN (Figure 3E) and the proposed mechanism involving REP.

claim: Rab26 not only preferentially associates with secretory vesicle clusters but actually induces their formation in a GTP-dependent manner.
source: Perhaps the most conspicuous feature of Rab26 is that it is not only preferentially associated with secretory vesicle clusters but actually induces their formation in a GTP-dependent manner as becomes apparent upon the expression of exogenous Rab26 variants in both neurons and non-neuronal cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing clustering with WT/QL versus TN variants in neurons (Figure 3, 6) and HeLa cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

claim: The weak homodimerization tendency of EGFP enhances the Rab26 clustering phenotype.
source: This is most dramatically observed with the EGFP-tagged variant suggesting that the weak homodimerization tendency of EGFP enhances the phenotype (note that no other EGFP-tagged Rab exhibits similar features including the most abundant secretory GTPase, Rab3a).
evidence: This is inferred from the more dramatic phenotype with EGFP-Rab26WT compared to FLAG-Rab26WT and the known dimerization properties of EGFP.

claim: No other EGFP-tagged Rab exhibits clustering features similar to EGFP-Rab26, including the most abundant secretory GTPase, Rab3a.
source: This is most dramatically observed with the EGFP-tagged variant suggesting that the weak homodimerization tendency of EGFP enhances the phenotype (note that no other EGFP-tagged Rab exhibits similar features including the most abundant secretory GTPase, Rab3a).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the authors' experience.

claim: It is unlikely that Rab26 clustering is effected by homophilic Rab26 interactions since the GTP-form of Rab26 does not oligomerize.
source: Nevertheless, since the GTP-form of Rab26 does not oligomerize, it is unlikely that clustering is effected by homophilic Rab26 interactions.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-IP data showing GTP-Rab26 does not oligomerize (Figure 2B) while clustering requires GTP-Rab26.

claim: Rab26-induced clustering is possibly mediated by a hitherto unknown effector protein.
source: Rather, it possible that clustering is mediated by a hitherto unknown effector protein.
evidence: This is speculated based on the GTP-dependence of clustering and the lack of GTP-Rab26 oligomerization.

claim: The effector mediating Rab26 clustering is probably distinct from Atg16L1.
source: This effector is probably distinct from Atg16L1 as overexpression of EGFP-Rab33B (that also recruits Atg16L1) does not induce such clusters (Figure 6, and data not shown).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that EGFP-Rab33B does not induce similar clusters despite also binding Atg16L1.

claim: The possibility that Atg16L1 mediates Rab26 clustering cannot be excluded given that the central terminal region of Atg16L1 has a tendency for homo-multimerization.
source: However, given that the central terminal region of Atg16L1 has a tendency for homo-multimerization, this possibility cannot be excluded (Mizushima et al., 2003; Ishibashi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on known properties of Atg16L1 from cited literature (Mizushima et al., 2003; Ishibashi et al., 2011).

claim: Overexpression of Rab26 in exocrine cell lines induces clustering of lysosomes.
source: Intriguingly, our findings agree with a recent report according to which overexpression of Rab26 in exocrine cell lines induces clustering of lysosomes, reminiscent of the partial co-localization of the EGFP-induced Rab26 clusters with lysosomes in neuronal cell bodies (Jin and Mills, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jin and Mills, 2014.

claim: Binding of Rab26 to Atg16L1 appears to be weaker than that between Rab33 and Atg16L1, which plays a role in canonical autophagy.
source: Interestingly, binding of Rab26 to Atg16L1 appears to be weaker than that between Rab33 and Atg16L1, which plays a role in canonical autophagy, probably explaining why Itoh et al. (2008) did not observe binding of GST-Rab26 to a full-length Atg16L1 protein using stringent conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the gel filtration results and explains discrepancy with previous work (Itoh et al., 2008).

claim: Itoh et al. (2008) did not observe binding of GST-Rab26 to a full-length Atg16L1 protein using stringent conditions.
source: Interestingly, binding of Rab26 to Atg16L1 appears to be weaker than that between Rab33 and Atg16L1, which plays a role in canonical autophagy, probably explaining why Itoh et al. (2008) did not observe binding of GST-Rab26 to a full-length Atg16L1 protein using stringent conditions.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Itoh et al., 2008.

claim: The interaction between Rab26 and Atg16L1 may be more transient or require additional factors for stabilization.
source: It is conceivable that the interaction is more transient, or else, that it requires additional factors for stabilization, thus allowing for fine-tuning the flow of synaptic vesicles targeted for selective autophagy.
evidence: This is speculated based on the weak binding observed and the biological context.

claim: Atg16L1 and Rab33A are associated with secretory vesicles in neuroendocrine PC12 cells.
source: In particular, Atg16L1 and Rab33A have recently been found to be associated with secretory vesicles in neuroendocrine PC12 cells, with the data suggesting a role for Atg16L1 in regulating exocytosis independent of autophagy (Ishibashi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ishibashi et al., 2012.

claim: Data suggest a role for Atg16L1 in regulating exocytosis independent of autophagy in PC12 cells.
source: In particular, Atg16L1 and Rab33A have recently been found to be associated with secretory vesicles in neuroendocrine PC12 cells, with the data suggesting a role for Atg16L1 in regulating exocytosis independent of autophagy (Ishibashi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ishibashi et al., 2012.

claim: The Rab26-Atg16L1 complexes in neurons represent pre-autophagosomal structures.
source: On the other hand, based on our extensive morphological assessment using double immunolabeling microscopy, we strongly favor that the Rab26-Atg16L1 complexes in neurons represent pre-autophagosomal structures because (i) Rab26 is not present on all synaptic vesicles but rather confined to vesicle aggregates that may be functionally impaired, and (ii) LC3 is recruited to these clusters suggesting that the formation of an autophagosomal membrane is, at least in part, initiated.
evidence: This is based on colocalization with Atg16L1 and LC3 (Figure 6), selective localization to vesicle clusters, and EM showing surrounding membranes (Figure 5).

claim: Rab26 is not present on all synaptic vesicles but rather confined to vesicle aggregates that may be functionally impaired.
source: On the other hand, based on our extensive morphological assessment using double immunolabeling microscopy, we strongly favor that the Rab26-Atg16L1 complexes in neurons represent pre-autophagosomal structures because (i) Rab26 is not present on all synaptic vesicles but rather confined to vesicle aggregates that may be functionally impaired, and (ii) LC3 is recruited to these clusters suggesting that the formation of an autophagosomal membrane is, at least in part, initiated.
evidence: This is demonstrated by partial colocalization with synaptic vesicle markers (Figure 3) and preferential association with clusters.

claim: LC3 recruitment to Rab26 clusters suggests that the formation of an autophagosomal membrane is, at least in part, initiated.
source: On the other hand, based on our extensive morphological assessment using double immunolabeling microscopy, we strongly favor that the Rab26-Atg16L1 complexes in neurons represent pre-autophagosomal structures because (i) Rab26 is not present on all synaptic vesicles but rather confined to vesicle aggregates that may be functionally impaired, and (ii) LC3 is recruited to these clusters suggesting that the formation of an autophagosomal membrane is, at least in part, initiated.
evidence: LC3 is a canonical autophagosome marker that is recruited during autophagosome formation, so its presence indicates initiation of autophagosome formation (Figure 6D).

claim: The vesicle clusters containing Rab26 and Atg16L1 have undergone exo-endocytotic cycling.
source: Our data indicates that the vesicle clusters containing Rab26 and Atg16L1 have undergone exo-endocytotic cycling.
evidence: This is demonstrated by labeling with luminal synaptotagmin-I antibody (Figure 3G).

claim: Clathrin has been shown to interact with Atg16L1, thus targeting plasma membrane constituents towards autophagosome precursors via clathrin-mediated endocytosis.
source: Intriguingly, clathrin has recently been shown to interact with Atg16L1, thus targeting plasma membrane constituents towards autophagosome precursors via clathrin-mediated endocytosis (Ravikumar et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ravikumar et al., 2010.

claim: Clathrin-mediated endocytosis constitutes the main endocytotic pathway for synaptic vesicles.
source: Since clathrin-mediated endocytosis constitutes the main endocytotic pathway for synaptic vesicles, it is conceivable that there is a synergy between Rab26- and clathrin-induced autophagocytosis in nerve terminals that further fine-tunes the targeting of synaptic vesicles to preautophagosomal structures.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about synaptic vesicle endocytosis.

claim: There may be synergy between Rab26- and clathrin-induced autophagocytosis in nerve terminals that fine-tunes the targeting of synaptic vesicles to preautophagosomal structures.
source: Since clathrin-mediated endocytosis constitutes the main endocytotic pathway for synaptic vesicles, it is conceivable that there is a synergy between Rab26- and clathrin-induced autophagocytosis in nerve terminals that further fine-tunes the targeting of synaptic vesicles to preautophagosomal structures.
evidence: This is speculated based on the known interaction between clathrin and Atg16L1 (Ravikumar et al., 2010) and the role of clathrin in synaptic vesicle endocytosis.

claim: Rab26 is a member of a signaling cascade that selectively targets synaptic and secretory vesicles towards autophagocytosis.
source: Taken together, the data support the view that Rab26 is member of a signaling cascade that selectively targets synaptic and secretory vesicles towards autophagocytosis, which may represent a novel and highly specific form of autophagy ('vesiculophagy').
evidence: This is concluded from the association with autophagy markers, selective localization to secretory vesicles, and functional data.

claim: Rab26-mediated targeting of vesicles to autophagy may represent a novel and highly specific form of autophagy termed 'vesiculophagy'.
source: Taken together, the data support the view that Rab26 is member of a signaling cascade that selectively targets synaptic and secretory vesicles towards autophagocytosis, which may represent a novel and highly specific form of autophagy ('vesiculophagy').
evidence: This is proposed based on the selective targeting of vesicles and the distinct mechanism from canonical autophagy.

claim: In addition to the classical, mTOR/ULK kinase-induced pathway of macroautophagy there is a panoply of diverse and highly regulated pathways (e.g., pexophagy and mitophagy) that all converge on the common pathway but differ in the mechanism of initiation and cargo recruitment.
source: In recent years, it has become apparent that in addition to the classical, mTOR/ULK kinase-induced pathway of macroautophagy there is a panoply of diverse and highly regulated pathways (e.g., pexophagy and mitophagy) that all converge on the common pathway but differ in the mechanism of initiation and cargo recruitment.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the autophagy field.

claim: In many selective autophagy pathways, the pathway is initiated by ubiquitination of target proteins.
source: In many of these cases the pathway is initiated by ubiquitination of target proteins.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about selective autophagy mechanisms.

claim: The initiation event for Rab26-mediated vesiculophagy may be the recruitment of active Rab26 to the membrane of subsets of synaptic vesicles.
source: While we do not know whether this is also the case here, it is conceivable that the initiation event may indeed be the recruitment of active Rab26 to the membrane of subsets of synaptic vesicles that then interacts with other factors to form clusters and to recruit an isolation membrane, the origin of which remains to be identified.
evidence: This is speculated based on the GTP-dependent association of Rab26 with vesicle clusters and autophagy machinery.

claim: Active Rab26 may interact with other factors to form clusters and recruit an isolation membrane.
source: While we do not know whether this is also the case here, it is conceivable that the initiation event may indeed be the recruitment of active Rab26 to the membrane of subsets of synaptic vesicles that then interacts with other factors to form clusters and to recruit an isolation membrane, the origin of which remains to be identified.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed clustering and membrane recruitment in the data.

claim: The origin of the isolation membrane recruited by Rab26 remains to be identified.
source: While we do not know whether this is also the case here, it is conceivable that the initiation event may indeed be the recruitment of active Rab26 to the membrane of subsets of synaptic vesicles that then interacts with other factors to form clusters and to recruit an isolation membrane, the origin of which remains to be identified.
evidence: This is stated as an open question for future research.
